::: {.lesson-eyebrow}
Explore · Lesson 1 of 6
:::

A completion rate looks like one number. Across `r fmt(nrow(four))` four-year institutions it is a shape, and the shape decides which summary you should report. This lesson is about seeing that shape before trusting any average.

**You will be able to:** read a histogram's shape, choose a bin width on purpose, decide between mean and median, and spot the floor, ceiling, and small-cohort effects that IPEDS rates carry.

## Watch it move {.beat data-beat="1 · Watch it move"}

Each dot is one four-year institution. Change the variable and the dots re-sort into the new histogram. Drag the bin count to see how much of the shape is the data and how much is your choice.

::: {.lab-anim}

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
inst = FileAttachment("data/institutions.csv").csv({typed: true})
four = inst.filter(d => d.level === "4-year")

metrics = new Map([
  ["6-year bachelor's completion (%)", "grad_rate_bach_6yr"],
  ["4-year bachelor's completion (%)", "grad_rate_bach_4yr"],
  ["Full-time retention (%)", "retention_ft"],
  ["Percent Pell", "pct_pell"],
  ["Net price ($)", "net_price"],
  ["Student-faculty ratio", "stu_fac_ratio"],
  ["12-month headcount", "headcount"]
])
```

::: {.lab-controls}
```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof metric = Inputs.select(metrics, {label: "Variable", value: "grad_rate_bach_6yr", width: 300})
viewof bins = Inputs.range([5, 60], {label: "Bins", step: 1, value: 20})
viewof logx = Inputs.toggle({label: "Log scale", value: false})
viewof marks = Inputs.checkbox(["Mean", "Median"], {label: "Show", value: ["Mean", "Median"]})
```
:::

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
histNode = d3.create("svg").attr("class", "lab-svg").node()

dotHist = {
  const width = 860, height = 400, margin = {top: 28, right: 16, bottom: 44, left: 16};
  const reduce = window.matchMedia("(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)").matches;
  const dur = reduce ? 0 : 750;
  const val = d => logx ? Math.log10(Math.max(d[metric], 1)) : d[metric];
  const rows = four.filter(d => d[metric] != null && Number.isFinite(d[metric]));
  const values = rows.map(val);
  const x = d3.scaleLinear().domain(d3.extent(values)).nice(bins).range([margin.left, width - margin.right]);
  const binned = d3.bin().domain(x.domain()).thresholds(x.ticks(bins)).value(val)(rows);
  const maxCount = d3.max(binned, b => b.length);
  const binW = x(binned[0].x1) - x(binned[0].x0);
  const plotH = height - margin.top - margin.bottom;
  const s = Math.min(9, Math.sqrt(binW * plotH / maxCount) * 0.97);
  const r = s / 2;
  const perRow = Math.max(1, Math.floor(binW / s));
  const pos = new Map();
  for (const b of binned) {
    const x0 = x(b.x0) + (binW - perRow * s) / 2;
    b.forEach((d, i) => {
      pos.set(d.unitid, {
        cx: x0 + r + (i % perRow) * s,
        cy: height - margin.bottom - r - Math.floor(i / perRow) * s
      });
    });
  }
  const fmt = metric === "net_price" ? d3.format("$,.0f") : metric === "headcount" ? d3.format(",.0f") : d3.format(".1f");
  const tickFmt = logx ? (v => d3.format("~s")(10 ** v)) : metric === "net_price" ? d3.format("$~s") : metric === "headcount" ? d3.format("~s") : d3.format("~f");
  const logTicks = dom => {
    const mults = dom[1] - dom[0] <= 2.5 ? [1, 2, 5] : dom[1] - dom[0] <= 4 ? [1, 3] : [1];
    const out = [];
    for (let e = Math.floor(dom[0]); e <= Math.ceil(dom[1]); e++) for (const m of mults) {
      const v = e + Math.log10(m);
      if (v >= dom[0] - 1e-9 && v <= dom[1] + 1e-9) out.push(v);
    }
    return out;
  };
  const raw = rows.map(d => d[metric]);
  const mean = d3.mean(raw), median = d3.median(raw);
  const toX = v => logx ? Math.log10(Math.max(v, 1)) : v;

  const svg = d3.select(histNode);
  svg.attr("viewBox", [0, 0, width, height]);
  let dots = svg.select("g.dots");
  if (dots.empty()) dots = svg.append("g").attr("class", "dots");
  let axis = svg.select("g.axis");
  if (axis.empty()) axis = svg.append("g").attr("class", "axis");
  let lines = svg.select("g.lines");
  if (lines.empty()) lines = svg.append("g").attr("class", "lines");

  axis.attr("transform", `translate(0,${height - margin.bottom})`)
    .transition().duration(dur)
    .call(d3.axisBottom(x).ticks(9).tickValues(logx ? logTicks(x.domain()) : null).tickFormat(tickFmt).tickSizeOuter(0));

  const t = svg.transition().duration(dur).ease(d3.easeCubicInOut);
  dots.selectAll("circle").data(rows, d => d.unitid)
    .join(
      enter => enter.append("circle").attr("r", 0).attr("fill", "var(--lab-primary)").attr("fill-opacity", 0.85)
        .attr("cx", d => pos.get(d.unitid).cx).attr("cy", height - margin.bottom - r)
        .call(e => e.append("title")),
      update => update,
      exit => exit.transition(t).attr("r", 0).remove()
    )
    .call(sel => sel.select("title").text(d => `${d.name}\n${fmt(d[metric])}`))
    .transition(t).delay((d, i) => reduce ? 0 : (i % 60) * 4)
    .attr("r", Math.max(1.2, r * 0.9))
    .attr("cx", d => pos.get(d.unitid).cx)
    .attr("cy", d => pos.get(d.unitid).cy);

  const markData = [
    {name: "Mean", v: mean, color: "var(--lab-accent)", dy: 0},
    {name: "Median", v: median, color: "var(--lab-ink)", dy: 14}
  ].filter(m => marks.includes(m.name));
  lines.selectAll("g.mark").data(markData, d => d.name)
    .join(
      enter => {
        const g = enter.append("g").attr("class", "mark");
        g.append("line").attr("y1", margin.top - 4).attr("y2", height - margin.bottom).attr("stroke-width", 2).attr("stroke-dasharray", "4 3");
        g.append("text").attr("font-size", 12).attr("font-weight", 700).attr("dx", 6);
        return g;
      },
      update => update,
      exit => exit.remove()
    )
    .each(function (m) {
      const g = d3.select(this);
      const mx = x(toX(m.v));
      g.select("line").attr("stroke", m.color).transition(t).attr("x1", mx).attr("x2", mx);
      g.select("text").attr("fill", m.color).attr("y", margin.top - 8 + m.dy)
        .text(`${m.name} ${fmt(m.v)}`)
        .attr("text-anchor", mx > width * 0.75 ? "end" : "start")
        .attr("dx", mx > width * 0.75 ? -6 : 6)
        .transition(t).attr("x", mx);
    });

  return svg.node();
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
readout = {
  const val = d => logx ? Math.log10(Math.max(d[metric], 1)) : d[metric];
  const rows = four.filter(d => d[metric] != null && Number.isFinite(d[metric]));
  const raw = rows.map(d => d[metric]);
  const mean = d3.mean(raw), median = d3.median(raw), sd = d3.deviation(raw);
  const skew = d3.mean(raw, v => ((v - mean) / sd) ** 3);
  const fmt = metric === "net_price" ? d3.format("$,.0f") : metric === "headcount" ? d3.format(",.0f") : d3.format(".1f");
  const shape = Math.abs(skew) < 0.3 ? "close to symmetric" : skew > 0 ? "right-skewed (long tail of high values)" : "left-skewed (long tail of low values)";
  return html`<div class="lab-readout">
    <div><span class="k">Institutions</span><span class="val">${d3.format(",")(rows.length)}</span></div>
    <div><span class="k">Missing</span><span class="val">${d3.format(",")(four.length - rows.length)}</span></div>
    <div><span class="k">Mean</span><span class="val accent">${fmt(mean)}</span></div>
    <div><span class="k">Median</span><span class="val">${fmt(median)}</span></div>
    <div><span class="k">Std. dev.</span><span class="val">${fmt(sd)}</span></div>
    <div><span class="k">Skewness</span><span class="val">${d3.format("+.2f")(skew)}</span></div>
  </div>
  <p class="lab-hint">Skewness is computed on the raw values, so it is the same with or without the log scale. This distribution is ${shape}.</p>`;
}
```

:::

Three things to try:

1. **Bins.** Push the bin count to 5, then to 60. At 5 the completion rate looks like a smooth hill; at 60 it is a comb. Neither is wrong. The question is what you want the reader to see.
2. **Headcount.** Switch to 12-month headcount. Almost every dot lands in the first bin because a few institutions enroll over 100,000 students. Turn on the log scale and the shape reappears. When the mean is far from the median, one of them is being dragged by a tail.
3. **Net price.** The mean sits above the median. That gap is the private institutions with very high prices pulling the average up, and it is why "average net price" in a press release and "typical net price" are not the same number.

## Do it {.beat data-beat="2 · Do it"}

The cells below run in your browser. Edit anything and press Run. The R and Python tabs do the same work; pick the one you use, or compare them.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

### R

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
#| caption: Load the institution table
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

inst <- read.csv("data/institutions.csv")
four <- inst |>
  filter(level == "4-year", !is.na(grad_rate_bach_6yr))

nrow(four)
```

The five-number summary plus the mean is the fastest read on a shape. If the mean and median differ by more than a few points, look for a tail.

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
#| caption: Summary statistics
four |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean = mean(grad_rate_bach_6yr),
    median = median(grad_rate_bach_6yr),
    sd = sd(grad_rate_bach_6yr),
    q25 = quantile(grad_rate_bach_6yr, 0.25),
    q75 = quantile(grad_rate_bach_6yr, 0.75),
    min = min(grad_rate_bach_6yr),
    max = max(grad_rate_bach_6yr)
  )
```

The histogram. Change `binwidth` and re-run. Try 2, 5, and 20.

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
#| caption: Histogram
ggplot(four, aes(grad_rate_bach_6yr)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, boundary = 0, fill = "#2a78d6", color = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean(four$grad_rate_bach_6yr), color = "#eb6834", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = median(four$grad_rate_bach_6yr), color = "#14213d", linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(
    x = "6-year bachelor's completion (%)", y = "Institutions",
    title = "Six-year completion at 4-year institutions",
    subtitle = "Solid line: mean. Dashed line: median."
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
```

One histogram hides three sectors. Faceting shows that the overall shape is really a mix of three different shapes.

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
#| caption: The same histogram by control
ggplot(four, aes(grad_rate_bach_6yr)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, boundary = 0, fill = "#2a78d6", color = "white") +
  facet_wrap(~ control, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "6-year bachelor's completion (%)", y = "Institutions") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
```

```{pyodide}
four["grad_rate_bach_6yr"].describe().round(1)
```

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: true

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.5))
ax.hist(rate, bins=range(0, 105, 5), color="#2a78d6", edgecolor="white")
ax.axvline(rate.mean(), color="#eb6834", linewidth=2, label=f"Mean {rate.mean():.1f}")
```

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: true

    ax.hist(grp["grad_rate_bach_6yr"], bins=range(0, 105, 5), color="#2a78d6", edgecolor="white")
```

::: {.lab-exercise data-exercise="eda1_median"}

### Median completion by control

The overall median hides the sectors. Return one row per `control` with the count of institutions and the **median** six-year completion rate, in a column named `median_rate`.

```{webr}
#| exercise: eda1_median
four |>
  group_by(______) |>
  summarise(n = n(), median_rate = ______(grad_rate_bach_6yr))
```

::: {.hint exercise="eda1_median"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint
The grouping column is `control`. The summary function you want is `median()`, not `mean()`.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="eda1_median"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution
```r
four |>
  group_by(control) |>
  summarise(n = n(), median_rate = median(grad_rate_bach_6yr))
```
Private nonprofits have the highest median, and for-profits the lowest, with the widest spread.
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: eda1_median
#| check: true
expected <- four |>
  dplyr::group_by(control) |>
  dplyr::summarise(median_rate = median(grad_rate_bach_6yr))
ok <- is.data.frame(.result) &&
  all(c("control", "median_rate") %in% names(.result)) &&
  nrow(.result) == 3 &&
  isTRUE(all.equal(sort(.result$median_rate), sort(expected$median_rate)))
if (ok) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct. Three sectors, three different medians. Compare them with the overall median from the summary cell above.")
} else if (is.data.frame(.result) && "median_rate" %in% names(.result)) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "The column is there but the values are off. Check that you grouped by control and used median().")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Not yet. The result should be a data frame with a column named median_rate.")
}
```

:::

::: {.lab-exercise data-exercise="eda1_small"}

### How many rates rest on tiny cohorts?

A completion rate on a cohort of 12 students moves 8 points when one student changes. Return the **share** (a number between 0 and 1) of four-year institutions in `four` whose bachelor's cohort, `bach_cohort`, is under 50 students.

```{webr}
#| exercise: eda1_small
mean(four$bach_cohort ______ 50, na.rm = TRUE)
```

::: {.hint exercise="eda1_small"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint
A logical vector's mean is the share of `TRUE` values. You need the comparison operator for "less than".
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="eda1_small"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution
```r
mean(four$bach_cohort < 50, na.rm = TRUE)
```
Roughly one in four four-year institutions computes its headline completion rate on fewer than 50 students. Any histogram of rates is partly a histogram of cohort sizes.
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: eda1_small
#| check: true
expected <- mean(four$bach_cohort < 50, na.rm = TRUE)
if (is.numeric(.result) && length(.result) == 1 && isTRUE(abs(.result - expected) < 1e-6)) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = sprintf("Correct: %.1f%% of these institutions have a bachelor's cohort under 50. Their rates are noisy by construction.", 100 * expected))
} else if (is.numeric(.result) && length(.result) == 1 &&
           (isTRUE(abs(.result - mean(four$bach_cohort >= 50, na.rm = TRUE)) < 1e-6) ||
            isTRUE(abs(.result - mean(four$bach_cohort > 50, na.rm = TRUE)) < 1e-6))) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "That is the share at or above 50. Flip the comparison.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Not yet. The answer is a single number between 0 and 1.")
}
```

:::

## In your stack {.beat data-beat="4 · In your stack"}

The same distribution in the tools most IR offices report from. The workbook [ir-lab.xlsx](data/ir-lab.xlsx) has the institution table and a `distributions` sheet already built.

::: {.panel-tabset group="stack"}

### Excel

The `distributions` sheet computes every statistic from the summary cell above with a filter on the Institutions table, so it updates if the data does. The array-style formulas need Excel 365 or 2021.

| Statistic | Formula |
|---|---|
| Count | `=COUNTIFS(Institutions[level],"4-year",Institutions[grad_rate_bach_6yr],"<>")` |
| Mean | `=AVERAGEIFS(Institutions[grad_rate_bach_6yr],Institutions[level],"4-year")` |
| Median | `=MEDIAN(IF(Institutions[level]="4-year",Institutions[grad_rate_bach_6yr]))` |
| Standard deviation | `=STDEV.S(IF(Institutions[level]="4-year",Institutions[grad_rate_bach_6yr]))` |
| Skewness | `=SKEW(IF(Institutions[level]="4-year",Institutions[grad_rate_bach_6yr]))` |
| 25th percentile | `=PERCENTILE.INC(IF(Institutions[level]="4-year",Institutions[grad_rate_bach_6yr]),0.25)` |

The frequency table uses one `COUNTIFS` per bin, with the bin edges in cells so you can change the width by editing two numbers:

```
=COUNTIFS(Institutions[level],"4-year",
          Institutions[grad_rate_bach_6yr],">="&D5,
          Institutions[grad_rate_bach_6yr],"<"&E5)
```

Excel's built-in Histogram chart (Insert, Statistic Chart) bins automatically but cannot filter, so it will silently include two-year institutions if you point it at the whole column. Point it at a filtered copy, or chart the `COUNTIFS` table as a column chart.

**Median by control**, the first exercise, is one `MEDIAN(IF())` per sector, or a PivotTable with `control` on rows if you are on a version without dynamic arrays. PivotTables offer average but not median, so the formula is the honest route.

### Power BI

::: {.ir-powerbi data-powerbi-page="distributions" data-powerbi-title="Completion distributions"}
**Interactive report: not connected yet.** Download the [Power BI project](data/ir-lab-powerbi.zip) to explore this lesson in Power BI Desktop. The embedded report will appear here once it is connected.
:::

Load `institutions.csv` with Get Data, or paste this into a blank query in the Advanced Editor:

```powerquery
let
    Source = Csv.Document(File.Contents("C:\path\to\institutions.csv"), [Delimiter = ",", Encoding = 65001, QuoteStyle = QuoteStyle.Csv]),
    Promoted = Table.PromoteHeaders(Source, [PromoteAllScalars = true]),
    Typed = Table.TransformColumnTypes(Promoted, {
        {"unitid", Int64.Type}, {"grad_rate_bach_6yr", type number}, {"bach_cohort", Int64.Type},
        {"net_price", Int64.Type}, {"pct_pell", type number}, {"headcount", Int64.Type}
    })
in
    Typed
```

Blanks arrive as `null`, which is what you want. Do not replace them with 0.

**Bins.** The quickest histogram is the built-in grouping: right-click `grad_rate_bach_6yr` in the Fields pane, choose New group, set Bin size to 5. That makes a column you can put on the axis of a clustered column chart with Count of unitid as the value. A calculated column gives you control over labels and sort order:

```dax
Completion Bin =
VAR r = institutions[grad_rate_bach_6yr]
VAR lo = MIN ( 95, FLOOR ( r, 5 ) )
RETURN IF ( ISBLANK ( r ), BLANK (), FORMAT ( lo, "0" ) & IF ( lo = 95, "–100", "–<" & FORMAT ( lo + 5, "0" ) ) )

Completion Bin Sort =
VAR r = institutions[grad_rate_bach_6yr]
RETURN IF ( ISBLANK ( r ), BLANK (), MIN ( 95, FLOOR ( r, 5 ) ) )
```

Bins are left-closed and right-open, except the final 95–100 bin includes 100%.

Set the sort-by column of `Completion Bin` to `Completion Bin Sort`, then filter the visual to `level = "4-year"`.

**Summary measures.** `MEDIAN` and `AVERAGE` ignore blanks. DAX has no skewness function, so it is one measure with the definition written out:

```dax
Median Completion = MEDIAN ( institutions[grad_rate_bach_6yr] )
Mean Completion   = AVERAGE ( institutions[grad_rate_bach_6yr] )

Completion Skewness =
VAR t = FILTER ( institutions, NOT ISBLANK ( institutions[grad_rate_bach_6yr] ) )
VAR m = AVERAGEX ( t, institutions[grad_rate_bach_6yr] )
VAR s = STDEVX.S ( t, institutions[grad_rate_bach_6yr] )
RETURN AVERAGEX ( t, POWER ( ( institutions[grad_rate_bach_6yr] - m ) / s, 3 ) )
```

A card visual for each, with a slicer on `control`, is the exercise above as a report page.

:::

## Before you leave

::: {.takeaways}
1. **The shape picks the summary.** Symmetric: mean and standard deviation. Skewed: median and quartiles. Report the one that describes the typical institution.
2. **Bin width is a choice, so make it on purpose.** Show a colleague two widths before settling on one, and say which you picked.
3. **A rate is only as steady as its denominator.** Filter or flag small cohorts before ranking anything.
4. **Facet before you conclude.** One histogram over three sectors is usually three histograms in a trench coat.
:::

Next in this track: **Missing on purpose**, on which blanks in IPEDS are structural, which are unreported, and who disappears when you drop them.
